opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core issue is that we've collapsed a really multidimensional question into a single number. Someone releases a model, it tops a leaderboard by half a point on some benchmark, and suddenly it's "the best model." But best at what, for whom, and at what cost?

There are a few layers to why I find it unreliable. The first is the benchmarks themselves. Many of them were designed years ago for a very different generation of models, and they've become saturated. There's also a real contamination problem: these datasets are all over the web, so there's a good chance models have seen the test questions during training. When you get a high score, you don't know if you're measuring capability or memorization.

The second layer is that the way we evaluate isn't standardized. Small changes in prompt formatting, the number of examples you give, or how you parse the output can shift results quite a bit. Two groups can evaluate the same model on the same benchmark and report different numbers. If that variance is bigger than the gap between models, the ranking doesn't tell you much.

The third, and the one I care about most, is what we leave out. We almost never report efficiency, energy use, or the compute it took to get that result. If one model is marginally more accurate but uses many times the energy per query, is it actually better? For a lot of real-world deployments, probably not. We also rarely look carefully at bias, how models behave across languages and communities, or how they fail. Those things matter enormously once a model is in people's hands.

So my argument is that evaluation should be more contextual and more holistic. Instead of asking "which model is best?", we should ask "which model is best for this task, under these constraints, with these trade-offs?" That means reporting multiple dimensions side by side, including cost and environmental impact, and being transparent about how evaluations were run so people can reproduce them. Otherwise leaderboards become more of a marketing tool than a scientific one.

r002.rationale: It says evaluation results can shift with prompt and parsing choices, and that groups evaluating the same model on the same benchmark can report different numbers, conveying poor reproducibility.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that "better" isn't really a well-defined concept. Better at what? For whom? In what context? When people say model X is better than model Y, what they usually mean is that it scored a few points higher on some benchmark, or that it climbed a couple of positions on a leaderboard. And then that number gets stripped of all its context and turned into this kind of universal claim of superiority, which it was never designed to support.

So part of my frustration is with how benchmarks get used, and part of it is with the benchmarks themselves. A lot of the standard evaluations we rely on were created years ago, often for a very different generation of models, and they've been reused and reused to the point where they've basically saturated. Everybody is at ninety-something percent, and the differences we're arguing about are within the noise. And on top of that, there's contamination. These datasets are on the internet, the models are trained on the internet, so you often can't tell whether a model is actually reasoning or whether it's seen the test questions before. That alone should make us very skeptical of a lot of the numbers we see.

Then there's the reproducibility problem. If you take the same model and the same benchmark and you run it with a slightly different prompt format, or a different number of few-shot examples, or a different way of parsing the answer, you can get results that differ by several points. So when a company reports a number in a technical report, I often have no way of knowing exactly how they got it, and when independent groups try to reproduce it, they frequently can't. That's not really science at that point. It's more like marketing with decimal points.

And I also think we're measuring a very narrow slice of what matters. We measure things like multiple-choice question answering, coding tasks, math problems, and those are fine, but they say very little about how a model behaves when it's actually deployed. They don't tell you about robustness across languages, about bias, about how it handles ambiguous or adversarial inputs, and they definitely don't tell you about the costs, whether that's the energy and compute it takes to run, or the broader social and environmental impact. Those things almost never show up on a leaderboard, and yet they're exactly what someone deciding whether to use a model in the real world should care about.

So when someone asks me which model is better, my honest answer is usually, I don't know, and neither does the leaderboard. I think we need evaluations that are more transparent about how they're run, that are harder to game, that are kept fresh so they don't saturate and leak into training data, and that reflect a much wider range of things we actually care about, including efficiency and impact. Until we have that, I'd treat most of these rankings as a very rough signal at best, and certainly not as a definitive answer to the question of which model is better.

r002.rationale: It says independent groups frequently cannot reproduce reported results and that small evaluation changes can shift scores.

r003.rationale: It identifies contamination: benchmark datasets are online, models train on online data, and models may have seen test questions before.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest problem is that we’ve started treating a benchmark score as if it tells us how good a model is in general. But it really tells us how that model performed on a particular set of questions, under particular conditions. And that might have very little to do with what you actually want to use it for.

There’s also the issue of data contamination. If we don’t know what a model was trained on, it’s hard to know whether those benchmark questions were in its training data. Are we measuring its ability to handle something new, or its ability to reproduce something it’s already seen?

Even when we ask people to compare outputs, what does “better” mean? A response can sound confident and be beautifully written and still be wrong. So I’d much rather ask: better for which task, for which users, and at what cost? I don’t think a single ranking can answer all of those questions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses benchmark scores and human comparisons, but does not describe comparing sampled model outputs with outputs from a fixed-label fine-tuned model as apples-to-oranges.

r002.rationale: It calls evaluation unreliable but does not state that results often cannot be reproduced when an evaluation is repeated.

r003.rationale: It identifies data contamination: benchmark questions may have appeared in a model’s training data, making it unclear whether evaluation measures new capability or recall.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest problem is that we’re treating “better” as if it were one thing. A model gets a higher score on a benchmark, and suddenly we say it’s the best model. But better at what? For whom? Under what conditions?

A lot of these benchmarks are multiple-choice questions or very narrowly defined tasks. They don’t necessarily reflect how people actually use language models. And when the benchmarks are public, there’s also the question of whether those questions have ended up in the training data. Are we measuring a model’s ability to generalize, or its ability to reproduce something it has already seen?

Then, even when you evaluate the same capability, the way you phrase the prompt can change the result. So a single score can give you this sense of precision without telling you how robust that result really is.

I’d much rather see evaluation tied to a particular use case, with several dimensions: how well the model works, where it fails, and what resources it takes to run. Those tradeoffs matter. A leaderboard position alone doesn’t tell you which model is the right choice.

r001.rationale: The response discusses benchmark scores and use cases, but does not compare sampled language-model outputs with a fixed-label fine-tuned model or call that comparison apples-to-oranges.

r002.rationale: It says prompt phrasing can change results, but does not state that evaluation results often cannot be reproduced when repeated.

r003.rationale: It identifies possible overlap between public benchmark questions and training data as a concern, asking whether evaluation measures generalization or reproduction of seen material.
